deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a continuous German prose text, apparently lecture or study notes on ancient Greek history. It follows on from the previous page (Thermopylae, Salamis, Plataea, Mycale) and continues on the next (Pausanias' fall, Athenian hegemony, the Delian League treasury). In order, the content is:

(1) After Mycale, the Greeks set themselves the aim of liberating the Greeks of Asia Minor, so the war went on for 30 more years.

(2) Once Greece was pacified within its borders, Athens had to be rebuilt (478). Themistocles planned to make Athens the first city of Greece by fortifying it and giving it a better harbour.

(3) Sparta opposed the fortification out of envy and jealousy. Themistocles used a ruse: he went to Sparta as envoy while work on the walls continued.

(4) Equally important was the building of the harbour Piraeus (477). It was fortified like the city and joined to it by long walls.

(5) In the Persian Wars Sparta had held the supreme command. Joint expeditions were undertaken to drive the Persians from the islands. One such expedition, under Pausanias (dated here 470), expelled the Persian garrisons from Cyprus and Byzantium. The sentence continues on fol. 81 with Pausanias' arrogance and the transfer of command to Athens.

There is nothing to reconstruct in modern mathematical notation. The handwriting is a rapid, rather schematic Kurrent and may not be Gauss's own. The bundle label 'HB.Lagrange1816' suggests these are notes bound or filed with other material, possibly by a student or family member, rather than Gauss's mathematical work.
errors: Historical, not mathematical: the Long Walls connecting Athens with Piraeus were built c. 461–456 BC, after Themistocles' ostracism. Attaching them to the Themistoclean Piraeus project of 477 conflates two phases. The Piraeus fortification itself was begun under Themistocles' archonship (493/2) and completed after 479.
Historical: Pausanias' expedition to Cyprus and Byzantium is usually dated 478 BC, not 470 as written.
The '30 more years' of war roughly matches the conventional end c. 449 BC (Peace of Callias), so it is acceptable as a rounded figure.

results.what: Narrative notes on Greek history 479–470 BC: rebuilding and fortification of Athens, Themistocles' ruse at Sparta, fortification of Piraeus, Pausanias' expedition to Cyprus and Byzantium.
results.modern_name: Pentekontaetia (the fifty years between the Persian and Peloponnesian Wars), standard ancient history
results.usually_credited_to: Thucydides I.89–95 (ancient source); standard 18th/19th-century textbooks such as Heeren's

deep.surprise_reason: The page is non-mathematical school or lecture notes on ancient Greek history, quite possibly not in Gauss's hand. It has no mathematical content and nothing of significance for the history of mathematics.

checkable.asserts: Trivial date check: 30 more years of war after 479 BC brings one to c. 449 BC, the conventional date of the Peace of Callias.
From the next page: 460 talents at 1200 florins per talent equals 552000 florins (context check only).
